# Introduction to the \(\SIR\) epidemic
In a population of fixed size, the \(\SIR\) epidemic runs under the following stochastic dynamics:

\begin{tabbing}
Infections \qquad \= \(S\to S-1\,, I \to I+1\) occur at rate \(\alpha \, S \, I\), \kill
\emph{Infections:} \> \(S\to S-1\,, I \to I+1\) occur at rate \(\alpha \, S \, I\), \\
\emph{Removals:}   \> \(I \to I-1\,, R \to R+1\)  occur at rate \(\beta \, I\).     
\end{tabbing}

The structural parameter of epidemic `duration` 
(a positive real number)
and the `initial` configuration
(of `SIR` type) are given by
`julia` constants,
as are the per-pair infection rate `α` and the per-individual rate of removal `β`.
The population size is computed as part of the construction of `initial`, producing an extra
mark obtained by computing the sum of 
its three fields 
(the non-negative integers supplied by the last three parameters of the `SIR` invocation).
```{julia}
const duration = 2.0;
const α, β = 0.2, 1.5;
const initial = SIR(0.0, 5, 1, 0);
```

```{julia}                                                                              
#| echo: false 
const MAXPOP = 20                                                                       
if initial.n > MAXPOP                                                                  
    circlabels = ["[$i]" for i in 1:initial.n]                                                                                         
else                                                                                    
    circlabels = [string(Char(codepoint('①') + i - 1)) for i in 1:initial.n]                                                           
end                                                                                     
function timelinelabels1(i) 
    if round(i) > 0 && i ≤ initial.n
        circlabels[round(Int, i)] 
    else
        "" 
    end 
end ;                                                                             
function timelinelabels2(i) 
    if i ≤ initial.n
        string(trunc(Int, i)) 
    else
        "" 
    end 
end ;                                                                             
```   

# Structure of potential infections and removals
Here is an example of a
structure recording times of potential incidents,
using convenient single-letter abbreviations
(potential infections `I`,
perpetuated infections `P`,
potential removals `R`
and conditioned removals `C`),
```{julia}
A = AbstractInfection;
I = Infection;      P = PInfection;
R = Removal;        C = CRemoval;

innovation = Innovation(initial.n,
    A[  I(0.11, 2, 3), I(0.2, 2, 5), P(0.4, 1, 2), I(0.5, 2, 5),  I(0.6, 2, 4), I(0.75, 1, 2), 
        I(0.85, 3, 4), I(0.9, 2, 3), I(1.0, 2, 5), I(1.05, 4, 5), I(1.1, 2, 3), P(1.2, 2, 4), 
        I(1.45, 4, 6), I(1.5, 3, 4),  I(1.6, 3, 5)  ],
    R[  R(0.3, 5), R(0.42, 3), R(0.7, 3), R(0.55, 3), R(0.95, 5), R(1.4, 2), R(1.55, 1),
        R(1.85, 2) ],
    C[  C(1.3, 2), C(0.8, 1), C(1.7, 4), C(1.8, 4), C(1.92, 5) ])
```
Incidents are displayed using corresponding script letters
(`I ≈ ℐ`, `P ≈ 𝒫`, `R ≈ ℛ`, `C ≈ 𝒞`).

# Constructing the epidemic
An epidemic is constructed by specifying a specific `initial` state
(an `SIR` structure)
at which the epidemic commences at time \(0.0\), and an `Innovations`
structure to hold subsequent (possibly) potential infections and removals.
The epidemic simulation is
simulated at construction of an instance
of the `Evolution` type, with `initial` as first argument
and a second argument `innovation` supplying subsequent potential incidents. 
@tbl-evolution tabulates the epidemic trajectory for `initial` and `innovation`.
```{julia}
#| label: tbl-evolution
#| tbl-cap: Table giving evolution of the epidemic
#| echo: false 
evolution = Evolution(initial, innovation)

flow = table_trajectories1(duration, initial, evolution.trajectory)
```

# Plotting the epidemic
We need graphical visualizations of
simulation of the epidemic
conditional on all activated removals being observed
(recall these are denoted by `C→𝒞`
representing "conditional removal");
with the ultimate objective of deriving a perfect simulation under this conditioning.
Note that the assumption of all activated removals being observed
is idealized, but not entirely unrealistic.

## The epidemic curve
First we draw the epidemic curve together with 
trajectories of removals and susceptibles (@fig-curves).
Incidentally, note that the epidemic curve peaks at two distinct
locations, as annotated in @fig-curves.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-curves
#| fig-cap: "Epidemic curve (with annotated peaks) together with monotonic \
#|           trajectories of numbers of susceptibles and removals."
curves_template = plot(flow, yintercept=1:initial.n,
    Geom.hline(style=:dash, size=0.1mm, color=theme.scaffold),
    Coord.cartesian(xmin=0, xmax=duration, ymin=0, ymax=initial.n + 0.25),
    Guide.xlabel("Process time", orientation=:horizontal),
    style(default_color=theme.background),
    gadfly_theme)

zero_layer = layer(flow, x=:t, y=:empty, Geom.line,
    style(line_width=2theme.trail, default_color=theme.scaffold))
push!(curves_template, zero_layer)

function new_figure(old_figure, gadfly_list...)
    figure = deepcopy(old_figure)
    push!(figure, gadfly_list...)
    return figure
end

figure1 = new_figure(curves_template, 
    Scale.y_continuous(labels=timelinelabels2),
    Guide.ylabel("Numbers of individuals"),
    Guide.title("Epidemic curve with removals and susceptibles"),
    layer(flow, x=:t, y=:infectives, Geom.step,
        style(line_width=theme.trail, default_color=theme.colour(I))),
    layer(flow, x=:t, y=:removals, Geom.step,
        style(line_style=[:dashdot], line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.colour(R))),
    layer(flow[flow.susceptibles.!=0, :], x=:t, y=:susceptibles, Geom.step,
        style(line_style=[:dash], line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.scaffold)),
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        text(1.2, 3.2, "Peak #1"),
        text(1.6, 3.2, "Peak #2"),
        fontsize(6pt)))
)
depict("introduction-curves", figure1)
```

## Plotting zone boundaries
For the coupling construction it is convenient to suppose the
various time lines are infected in increasing index order (re-labelling symmetry
means the statistics of the
evolutions of total numbers of `susceptibles`, `infectives` and `removals` are not affected).
Thus the epidemic is now defined by boundaries between a _removals zone_ and
an _infectivity zone_, and between the infectivity zone and a _susceptible zone_.
This is illustrated in @fig-boundary.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-boundary
#| fig-cap: "Time-evolving boundaries between susceptible, infected,     \
#|           and removed sub-populations. Note that the boundary between \
#|           susceptible and infected is itself infected; similarly the  \
#|           boundary between infected and removed is itself removed."
incidents_template = new_figure(curves_template,
    Scale.y_continuous(labels=timelinelabels1),
    Guide.yticks(ticks=collect(1:(initial.n))),
    Guide.ylabel("Time lines")
)

figure2a = new_figure(incidents_template,
    layer(flow, x=:t, y=:removals, Geom.step,
        style(line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.colour(R))),
    layer(flow, x=:t, y=:epidemic, Geom.step,
        style(line_width=theme.trail, default_color=theme.colour(I))),
    layer(flow, x=:t, y=:population, Geom.line,
        style(line_width=theme.trail, default_color=theme.scaffold))
)

figure2 = new_figure(incidents_template,
    layer(flow, x=:t, y=:removals, Geom.step,
        style(line_width=theme.boundary, default_color=theme.colour(R))),
    layer(flow, x=:t, y=:epidemic, Geom.step,
        style(line_width=theme.trail, default_color=theme.colour(I)))
)

depict("introduction-boundary", 
    new_figure(figure2a,
        Guide.title("Boundaries for the coupling construction"))
)
```

## Plotting infectivity and removed zones
Space-time zones of infection and removal
use a blend of the original data frame with lagged data
(tabulated in @tbl-evolution-enhanced).
The actual zones of infectivity and removals (@fig-zones)
are closed at their upper boundaries: the top edge of
the infectivity region is to be considered as _infected_
so long as this is not also the top of the removals region, 
the top end of the removal region is to be considered as _removed_.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-zones
#| fig-cap: "Infectivity and removal zones."
xyflow = table_trajectories2(flow, theme=theme) ;

figure3 = new_figure(figure2,
    layer(xyflow, x=:t, ymin=:empty, ymax=:removals, Geom.ribbon,
        alpha=[2theme.opacity], style(default_color=theme.colour(R))),
    layer(xyflow, x=:t, ymin=:removals, ymax=:epidemic, Geom.ribbon,
        alpha=[theme.opacity], style(default_color=theme.colour(I))),
)
depict("introduction-zones", new_figure(figure3,
    Guide.title("Zones of infectivity and removal"))
)
```
```{julia}
#| label: tbl-evolution-enhanced
#| tbl-cap: Enhanced table giving evolution of the epidemic
#| echo: false
xyflow
```

## Adding incidents to the plot
We now add incidents corresponding to the underlying `innovation`
using the `EpidemicsUtilities` function `draw_elements`:
see @fig-incidents.
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-incidents
#| fig-cap: "Incidents arising from the `Innovation` structure,              \
#|           together with the epidemic curve and infectivity and             \
#|           removal zones. Note that most of these incidents are inactive.  \
#|           The zones are closed at their upper edges: the upper boundary   \
#|           of the infectivity zone is \"infected\",            \
#|           while the upper boundary of the removal zone is \"removed\"."
figure4 = new_figure(figure3,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_elements(innovation; theme=theme))),
)
depict("introduction-incidents", new_figure(figure4,
    Guide.title("Incidents driving the epidemic"))
)
```

## Indicating activated incidents
Only some of these incidents are actually activated by the construction:

 * _Infections_ (`I ≈ ℐ` and `P ≈ 𝒫`) must lie inside the infectivity zone with
 infectee marks reaching 
 up to the time line which at that point of time is immediately above
 the infectivity zone (and hence must reach exactly
 one time line above the highest infected time line);
 * _Removals_ (`R ≈ ℛ` and `C ≈ 𝒞`) must lie inside the infectivity zone.

This is illustrated in @fig-activated, where the activated incidents
are emphasized by being drawn using thicker lines.
Note that perpetuated infections (`P ≈ 𝒫`) will arise
as part of the algorithmic time evolution of the entire \(\SIR\) trajectory.
Conditioned removals (`R ≈ ℛ`)
are the _only_ removals which should be activated: if an ordinary removal
(`R ≈ ℛ`) is activated then this breaks the conditioning (on all
observed removals) that we have imposed.

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-activated
#| fig-cap: "Activated incidents (thicker lines) driving the epidemic:          \
#|           notice that activated removals are exactly those removals lying \
#|           in the infectivity zone, while activated infections are exactly  \
#|           those infections reaching from within the infectivity zone to   \
#|           just above it."

figure5 = new_figure(figure4,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_activated_elements(initial, evolution.history, theme=theme)))
)
depict("introduction-activated", new_figure(figure5,
    Guide.title("Incidents driving the epidemic, emphasizing activated incidents"))
)
```

# Evolving the epidemic in algorithmic time
We can now give a visual explanation of how to evolve
an \(\SIR\) epidemic _in algorithmic time_,
subject to conditioning
on observed (conditioned) removals.
A single step of algorithmic time evolution can be broken down into a number of sub-steps:

1. Sample a new `Innovation` structure with fixed times for the conditional removals;
2. Remove all unconditioned removals
(those removals not activated, denoted by `R ≈ ℛ`);
3. Insert precisely those removals from the new `Innovation` 
structure which will not be activated
(equivalently, which do not lie in the infectivity zone);
4. Re-sample proposed time lines for each of the conditioned removals
(denoted by `C ≈ 𝒞`),
accepting proposals for which the relevant conditioned removal 
is still in the infectivity zone; 
5. Now work from right to left, deciding for each old infection incident from the new `Innovation`
whether it is to be removed, and for each new infection incident from the new `Innovation`
whether it is to be introduced:
   - an old infection incident is removed unless so doing 
 would result in a conditioned removal (`C ≈ 𝒞`) _not_ being removed. 
 If that
 turns out to be the case, then the old infection incident is retained
 but converted into a _perpetuated_ infection (`P ≈ 𝒫`);
   - a new infection incident is introduced unless so doing would
 result in a potential (but not activated / conditioned) removal (`R ≈ ℛ`)
 being activated.
 If that
 turns out to be the case, then the new infection incident is not introduced.
 

We will then need to address two issues. _Firstly_, we will need a convenient way of organizing 
the calculations required for making the decisions in item 5;
_Secondly_, we will need to show that the algorithmic time evolution is monotonic in some useful sense
that allows us to carry out a CFTP simulation,

## Sample a new `Innovation` structure
We first must produce a randomly sampled innovation with conditioned removals
occurring at the same times (using the function `generate_innovation`) but using different time lines,
then by producing a new innovation for which the conditioned removals are obtained by altering the
time lines for the conditioned removals of the template `Innovation`. Recall the original innovation:
```{julia}
#| echo: false
innovation
```
This will be amended based on a completely new randomly-sampled `Innovation`: 
```{julia}
new_innovation = generate_innovation(innovation, duration, α=α, β=β)
```
Clearly we cannot simply replace `innovation` by `new_innovation`, as this will break the conditioning.
Instead we have to consider each change (removal of old incident, introduction of new incident,
replacing old by new conditioned removal mark) individually, to see if this breaks the conditioning.

::: {.callout-warning}
# An important expositional point
Evidently some care has to be taken to insure that individual changes satisfy the requirements
of some kind of generalized detailed balance condition, in order to be assured that the changes
preserve the conditional distribution of the \(\SIR\) epidemic. This should be discussed carefully 
in the paper now being drafted: it is one of the crucial steps of the entire argument!
:::

## Remove all inactive removals from initial `Evolution`
We first modify the original `innovation` by removing all unactivated removals 
(since these will automatically be rejected).
The corresponding evolution is plotted in @fig-old-removals-gone, which is actually
a simple modification of @fig-activated. 
```{julia}
innovation0 = Innovation(initial.n, innovation.infections, R[], innovation.cremovals)
evolution0 = Evolution(initial, innovation0)
```
```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-old-removals-gone
#| fig-cap: "This is @fig-activated, but with all non-activated removals taken away, \
#|           while conditioned removals are retained."

figure6 = new_figure(figure3,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_elements(innovation0, theme=theme))),
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_activated_elements(initial, evolution0.history, theme=theme)))
)
depict("introduction-old-removals-gone", new_figure(figure6,
    Guide.title("The epidemic as before, deleting all non-activated removals"))
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
# Deleted inactive removals cannot affect epidemic
We emphasize that the deleted removals are all inactive, so that the epidemic trajectory
will not be affected by this step.
:::


## Adding in removals from the new innovation which will be inactive
We now insert removals from `new_innovation` which will not be activated by the old epidemic structure. 
To do this, we need first to compute the "birth" and "death" times of the infection for each time line
(note that we assume _every_ time line dies at the largest time `duration`: we could have tried
to use an infinite number `Inf`, but `duration` is algorithmically 
convenient!)
```{julia}
function life_dates(ev)
    start, finis = evolution.trajectory[1], evolution.trajectory[end]
    # Compute birth times
    births = sort([z.t for z in evolution0.history if typeof(z) <: AbstractInfection])
    prepend!(births, repeat([0.0], start.i + start.r))
    append!(births, repeat([duration], finis.s))
    # Compute death times
    deaths = sort([z.t for z in evolution0.history if typeof(z) <: AbstractRemoval])
    prepend!(deaths, repeat([0.0], start.r))
    append!(deaths, repeat([duration], finis.i + finis.s))
    # Check same number of births as deaths
    if length(births) != length(deaths)
        error("the numbers of births and deaths, $(length(births)) and $(length(deaths)), are not equal ")
    end

    return (births, deaths)
end

function inactive_removals(ev, innov)
    t0, t1 = life_dates(ev)
    return [z for z in innov.removals if !(t0[z.target] ≤ z.t < t1[z.target])]
end

inactive_removals(evolution, new_innovation)
```
So now we must add the inactive removals from `new_innovation` to `innovation0` to form
a resulting (intermediate) evolution which is plotted in @fig-inactive-removals.
```{julia}
innovation1 = Innovation(initial.n, innovation0.infections, 
                    inactive_removals(evolution, new_innovation),
                    innovation0.cremovals)
evolution1 = Evolution(initial, innovation1)
```

::: {.callout-note}
# Introduction of inactive removals cannot affect epidemic
We emphasize that the new removals are all inactive, so that the epidemic trajectory
will not be affected by this step.
:::

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-inactive-removals
#| fig-cap: "This is @fig-old-removals-gone, but with non-activated removals added \
#|           from `new_innovation`."
figure7 = new_figure(figure3,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_elements(innovation1, theme=theme))),
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_activated_elements(initial, evolution1.history, theme=theme)))
)
depict("introduction-inactive-removals", new_figure(figure7,
    Guide.title("Inactive removals added from new innovation"))
)
```

## Re-sampling using proposed time lines for conditioned removals
Now consider the conditioned removals. Compare the old and new conditioned removals
```{julia}
println(sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), innovation.cremovals))
println(sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), innovation1.cremovals))
```
to see whether the old can be replaced by the corresponding new conditioned removal.
This happens if the new conditioned removal is still be activated in
the simulation, which happens if it lies in the infectivity zone given by the corresponding
interval formed from
```{julia}
t0, t1 = life_dates(evolution1)
show(collect(zip(t0, t1)))
```

The results of this accept/reject phase can now be computed:
we compare original conditional removals with the proposal
and also with the result of the accept/reject stage.
```{julia}
function accept_reject(old_cremoval, proposed_cremoval, t0, t1)
    t, k = proposed_cremoval.t, proposed_cremoval.target
    return t0[k] ≤ t ≤ t1[k] ? proposed_cremoval : old_cremoval
end

function resulting_cremovals(innovation, new_innovation, t0, t1)
    [accept_reject(oldcr, propcr, t0, t1) 
        for (oldcr, propcr) in zip(innovation.cremovals, new_innovation.cremovals)]
end

println(rpad("original cremovals:", 25, " "), sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), 
    innovation.cremovals),
    rpad("\nproposed cremovals:", 25, " "), sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"),
    new_innovation.cremovals),
    rpad("\nresulting cremovals:", 25, " "), sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), 
    resulting_cremovals(innovation, new_innovation, life_dates(evolution1)...)))
```

@fig-processed-cremovals graphs the resulting evolution.
```{julia}
innovation2 = Innovation(initial.n, innovation1.infections, 
                    innovation1.removals, 
                    resulting_cremovals(innovation, new_innovation, life_dates(evolution1)...))
evolution2 = Evolution(initial, innovation2)
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-processed-cremovals
#| fig-cap: "This is @fig-inactive-removals, but with accept/reject applied  to  \
#|           `cremoval` marks. Under the current seed (`2`) only the first       \
#|           conditioned removal (at time $0.80$) has actually had its mark    \
#|           changed (from $1$ to $2$)." 
figure8 = new_figure(figure3,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_elements(innovation2, theme=theme))),
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_activated_elements(initial, evolution2.history, theme=theme)))
)
depict("introduction-processed-cremovals", new_figure(figure8,
    Guide.title("Marks for conditioned removals changed by accept/reject"))
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
# Accepted mark changes for conditional removals cannot affect epidemic
All conditional removals remain active, so that the epidemic trajectory
will not be affected by this step.
:::

## Removing old infection incidents and introducing new infection incidents where suitable
To carry out the next task we need to make some prior computations:

a) Compute the latest feasible epidemic curve. 
We do this using new infections occurring _later_ than the previous epidemic curve
(working in reverse time);
but perpetuating active infections when there is nothing useful occurring later;
b) For each time line, compute the last inactive removal occurring prior to the
activated infection on that time line;
c) Now work through new infections occurring _earlier_ than the previous epidemic curve
(working in reverse time again)
but rejecting those which would lead to activation of a previously unactivated removal.

### The latest feasible epidemic curve
Compare the active and inactive infections from the original `Evolution` structure
with those of the new `Innovation` structure:
```{julia}
#| echo: false
println(
    rpad("old infections:", 20, " "), 
        sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), evolution.infections),
    rpad("new infections:", 20, " "), 
        sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), new_innovation.infections)
)
```
@fig-with-all-new-infections displays the infection incidents from `new_innovation` 
superimposed on removals, active infections and epidemic and removal boundaries from @fig-processed-cremovals. Note that the new infection incidents have not yet been used to determine the 
new epidemic trajectory!

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-with-all-new-infections
#| fig-cap: "This displays _all_ the new infections from `new_innovation`                 \
#|           (in pink outline with no text),                                              \
#|           but retains removals and activated infections from @fig-processed-cremovals."
figure9 = new_figure(figure3,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
         draw_feasible_incident(new_innovation.infections, 1, inscribe=false, theme=theme))),
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_activated_elements(initial, evolution2.history, theme=theme))),
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_incident(evolution2.history, theme=theme))),
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
        draw_incident(evolution2.removals, theme=theme))),
)
depict("introduction-processed-cremovals", new_figure(figure9,
    Guide.title("New infections superimposed"))
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
# Note on exposition
Revise the following to achieve more clarity.
:::

The latest feasible epidemic is the slowest possible chain of activated infections that triggers all of the conditioned removals of `evolution2`,
and this is achieved so long as the proposed chain triggers those 
conditional removals for which the `target` field delivers
an increase in the running supremum.
This observation helps us to consider which 
of the new infections
```{julia}
#| echo: false
new_innovation.infections
```
are relevant
to construction of the latest feasible epidemic. 
For such an infection, the `target` mark must lie in the infectious
zone, and the `infectee` mark must not lie below the most recent running supremum.

The relevant infections are computed by the following function,
and are depicted in @fig-with-relevant-infections.
```{julia}
function relevant_infections(ev, innov)
    t0, t1 = life_dates(ev)
    relevant_infections = [z for z in ev.history if typeof(z) <: AbstractInfection]
    rsup, running_supremum_list = 0, CRemoval[]
    for z in sort(union(ev.cremovals, innov.infections),lt=isearlier)
        if (typeof(z) == CRemoval) && (z.target > rsup)
            push!(running_supremum_list, z)
            rsup = z.target
        elseif typeof(z) <: AbstractInfection && t0[z.target] ≤ z.t < t1[z.target] && z.infectee > rsup
            push!(relevant_infections, z)
        end
    end
    return sort(relevant_infections, lt=isearlier)
end
relev = relevant_infections(evolution2, new_innovation)
println("Relevant infections: ", sprint(show, MIME("text/plain"), relev))
```

```{julia}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-with-relevant-infections
#| fig-cap: "This improves on @fig-with-all-new-infections by adding the _relevant_      \
#|           infections from `new_innovation` (coloured in hot-pink outline with text)."
relev = relevant_infections(evolution2, new_innovation)
figure10 = new_figure(figure9,
    Guide.annotation(compose(context(),
         draw_feasible_incident(relev, 2, theme=theme))),
)
depict("introduction-processed-cremovals", new_figure(figure10,
    Guide.title("Relevant new infections are emphasized"))
)
```
